You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Clinical prediction models are being developed and used in the diagnosis of neonatal sepsis. Give me a summary of the predictors that are used in the models included in the study. Emphasize the numbers and percentages.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

content:
1	Clinical prediction models to diagnose neonatal sepsis in low-income and middle-income
     2	 countries: a scoping review
     3	
     4	
     5	 Neonatal sepsis causes significant morbidity and mortality worldwide but is difficult to diagnose
     6	 clinically. Clinical prediction models (CPMs) could improve diagnostic accuracy. Neonates in
     7	lowincome and middle-income countries are disproportionately affected by sepsis, yet no review has
     8	 comprehensively synthesised CPMs validated in this setting. We performed a scoping review of
     9	 CPMs for neonatal sepsis diagnosis validated in low-income and middle-income countries. From
    10	 4598 unique records, we included 82 studies validating 44 distinct models. Most studies were set in
    11	 neonatal intensive or special care units in middle-income countries and included neonates already
    12	 suspected of sepsis. Three quarters of models were only validated in one study. Our review
    13	 highlights several literature gaps, particularly a paucity of studies validating models in
    14	low-income
    15	 countries and the WHO African region, and models for the general neonatal population.
    16	 Furthermore, heterogeneity in study populations, definitions of sepsis and reporting of models may
    17	 hinder progress in this field.
    18	
    19	
    20	 METHODS
    21	 We conducted this review according to an a priori published protocol,15 developed with reference to
    22	 the scoping review guidelines provided by the Joanna Briggs Institute.16 We report methods and
    23	 results in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses
    24	 extension for Scoping Reviews (see supplementary appendix).17
    25	 Search strategy
    26	 Eligibility criteria are shown in Table 1. After reviewing the extent and breadth of the literature
    27	from
    28	 our initial searches, we narrowed the scope of our original protocol to focus specifically on
    29	studies
    30	 that validate a CPM to diagnose neonatal sepsis in a LMIC, as defined by the World Bank in 2020.
    31	 18
    32	 We searched six electronic databases from their inception: Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, Scopus,
    33	 Web of Science Core Collection, Global Index Medicus, and the Cochrane Library. Searches were
    34	 initially performed on 20 December 2019 and updated on 5 September 2022 and 16 June 2024.
    35	 Search terms were chosen to capture the three domains of the research question (‘neonate’,
    36	 ‘sepsis’, and ‘clinical prediction model’) through collaboration with a child health specialist
    37	librarian.
    38	 The search strategy was developed for Ovid MEDLINE and adapted for each database (see
    39	 supplementary appendix). Additional studies were identified by citation analysis and by hand
    40	 searching the reference lists of included studies.
    41	 Record screening
    42	 We imported identified records into EndNote 21 for deduplication.19 Unique records were then
    43	 uploaded to the Rayyan application for screening by two independent reviewers (DM, HG, MZ, SRN
    44	 or SS).
    45	 20 Titles and abstracts were first examined against the eligibility criteria to determine if each
    46	 record was potentially eligible for inclusion. Next, full texts of potentially eligible studies
    47	were
    48	 obtained and reviewed to confirm eligibility. Authors were contacted to request full texts where
    49	 these could not be found online. Conflicts were resolved by discussion amongst the review team.
    50	 Data extraction and synthesis
    51	 Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers for the initial searches (SRN and SS)
    52	 and by one reviewer for each updated search (SRN or SS). We extracted data on study, participant
    53	 and model characteristics, and model performance using a pre-piloted data extraction form (see
    54	 supplementary appendix). Data items were chosen based on the Transparent Reporting of a
    55	 multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement.21 We
    56	 summarised results by narrative synthesis. Data for quantitative outcomes were not pooled in a
    57	 meta-analysis as this is beyond the scoping review methodology. Where multiple variations of a
    58	 model were presented in the same study (e.g. different combinations of predictors presented during
    59	 model specification), or model performance was presented at multiple classification thresholds, we
    60	 only included data for the ‘optimal’ or ‘final’ model at a single classification threshold.
    61	
    62	
    63	 RESULTS
    64	 Searches and included studies
    65	 Searches identified 4598 unique records (Figure 1). From these, 82 studies published between 2003
    66	 and 2024 were included,
    67	 22-103 and are summarised in Tables 2 and 3. The number of published
    68	 studies validating a CPM to diagnose neonatal sepsis in LMICs has increased rapidly in recent years
    69	 (Figure 2). Studies were conducted in 22 individual countries (Figure 3 and Table 4), with the
    70	 greatest number of studies conducted in the World Health Organization (WHO) South-East Asian Region
    71	(n=48, 59%), particularly in India (n=37, 45%). The fewest studies were conducted in the
    72	 WHO African Region (n=4, 5%). Regarding economic status, 51 studies were conducted exclusively in
    73	 lower middle-income countries (62%) and 30 exclusively in upper middle-income countries (37%).
    74	 One study pooled data from both low-income and lower middle-income countries.98 Most studies
    75	 were set in intensive care or special care admission units (n=64, 78%). The remainder included all
    76	 live births at study sites (n=12, 15%), neonates presenting to emergency care services (n=3, 4%),
    77	all
    78	 hospitalised neonates (n=1, 1%), or the setting was unclear (n=2, 2%).
    79	 In total, 24252 neonates were included across all studies. The median number of participants per
    80	 study was 151 (range 36 to 3303, interquartile range [IQR] 200). Few studies restricted the study
    81	 population based on gestational age or birthweight, with only 4 studies (5%) specifically
    82	investigating
    83	 preterm neonates and 5 studies (6%) specifically investigating low or very low birthweight
    84	neonates.
    85	 Most studies included neonates clinically suspected of sepsis or with specific maternal risk
    86	factors
    87	 including chorioamnionitis (n=58, 71%).
    88	 Almost all studies included a positive blood and/or CSF culture in their outcome definition for
    89	sepsis
    90	 (n=75, 91%). Of these, 18 (22% of all studies) also included clinical features or clinical
    91	suspicion of
    92	 sepsis. One study used a consultant neonatologist’s clinical diagnosis of sepsis,
    93	 76 one study used the
    94	 International Classification of Diseases 10th Revision criteria for sepsis,77 and in three studies
    95	the
    96	 outcome was unclear.
    97	
    98	
    99	 Model characteristics
   100	 The 82 included studies performed 109 evaluations validating 44 distinct models (Table 3).22-
   101	 25,32,33,40,46,47,49-51,54,56,57,63,68,72,76-78,81,83,86,87,90,92,98-101,103-113 The most
   102	frequently validated model was the
   103	 Hematological Scoring System by Rodwell et al. (n=32, 39% of studies; including studies that made
   104	 minor modifications to the original model).112 Most models were only validated in one study (n=34,
   105	 77% of models).
   106	 A total of 135 predictors of sepsis were included across all models, of which 82 were clinical
   107	 parameters (signs, symptoms or risk factors) and 53 were laboratory parameters (see supplementary
   108	 appendix). The median number of predictors per model was 6 (range 2 to 110, IQR 4). 14 models

109	 (32%) included only clinical parameters, 12 models (27%) included only laboratory parameters, and
   110	 18 models (41%) included both. The commonest laboratory parameters were white cell count (n=17
   111	 models, 39%), C-reactive protein (CRP) (n=16 models, 36%) and platelet count (n=15 models, 34%).
   112	 The commonest clinical parameters were neonatal fever (n=13 models, 30%) and gestational age
   113	 (n=11 models, 25%).
   114	 Most models were developed using logistic regression (n=16 models, 36%) (often with stepwise
   115	 selection to select predictors) or consisted of a scoring system based on univariable predictor
   116	 performance or literature review and expert opinion (n=10 models, 23%).
